summary_ja: 期待エクスポージャー方式の承認基準として、モデルの一年以上の内部管理での運用と、独立した管理部署、ストレス・テスト、モデル検証（IMMバック・テスティング）、取締役等の関与、内部監査、担保管理、誤方向リスク管理、クロス・プロダクト・ネッティングの要件等を定める。
summary_en: Approval standards for the internal model method: at least a year of internal use, an independent CCR control unit, stress testing (incl. wrong-way and reverse stress tests), model validation with IMM backtesting, board involvement, internal audit, collateral management, wrong-way risk controls and cross-product netting requirements.

terms.ja: 期待エクスポージャー管理部署

paragraphs: When the Commissioner of the Financial Services Agency intends to grant the approval under Article 49, paragraph (1) for the use of the expected exposure method, the Commissioner shall examine whether the expected exposure model has been operated in internal management for at least one year before that approval, and whether, on and after the date on which use of the expected exposure method begins, the internal management framework is expected to conform to the following standards. (i) That the unit responsible for designing and operating the framework for managing counterparty credit risk (meaning credit risk to counterparties of derivative transactions, repo-style transactions, etc.; the same applies hereinafter in this Article) (hereinafter referred to in this Article as the "expected exposure management unit") is established independently of the units involved in the transactions for which credit risk-weighted assets are calculated. (ii) That the expected exposure management unit carries out appropriate stress tests and, for the expected exposure model, analyses the difference between expected exposure and the actual exposure amount that would arise if changes in risk factors exceeding the assumptions about future changes in risk factors occurred. (iii) That, in carrying out the stress tests in the preceding item, all of the following requirements are satisfied: (a) All forms of transactions carrying counterparty credit risk are captured for each counterparty over a sufficient period. (b) Changes in exposures arising from the main market risk factors, such as interest rates, foreign exchange, share prices, commodity prices and credit spreads, are analysed monthly and concentrations in sensitivities are identified. (c) Changes in exposures assuming the effects of multiple factors (including the occurrence of severe economic conditions and market movements, a broad decline in market liquidity, and the unwinding of positions by core market participants) are analysed at least once every three months, and non-directional risk (meaning yield curve exposures and basis risk) is assessed. (d) Stress tests that simultaneously consider changes in exposures affected by deteriorating economic conditions, etc. and a decline in counterparties' creditworthiness are analysed at least once every three months. (e) Stress tests considering the factors provided in (b) through (d) are carried out at the level of the counterparty, of groupings of counterparties, or of all counterparties combined. (f) Scenarios for risk factors include at least the following: (1) Scenarios assuming deterioration of the market environment experienced in the past. (2) Scenarios reflecting reasonable but severe stress. (3) Scenarios whose impact is limited but in which losses are more likely to occur. (g) To identify general wrong-way risk, stress scenarios are prepared that specify risk factors positively correlated with the counterparty's creditworthiness. (h) Reverse stress tests (meaning stress tests for identifying stress scenarios that are highly likely to have a serious impact on management and are plausible) are carried out. (i) The results of stress tests are incorporated into credit risk management procedures, and appropriate responses to excessive concentrations or concentrated risks are taken based on regular reporting to directors, etc. (j) Documents describing the procedures for carrying out stress tests have been prepared. (iv) That the expected exposure management unit carries out, independently of the development of the expected exposure model, validation of the accuracy of the expected exposure model and of the risk indicators generated from it (meaning indicators measured as effective EPE and as components of effective EPE that are important for risk management; the same applies hereinafter in this Article) (hereinafter referred to in this Article as "model validation"). (v) That, in carrying out model validation, all of the following requirements are satisfied: (a) It is carried out when the expected exposure model is developed and periodically thereafter. (b) IMM backtesting (meaning comparison of risk indicators calculated by the expected exposure model with actual measured values, and comparison of changes in hypothetical risk indicators based on fixed positions with actual measured values; the same applies in (h)) and other appropriate validation methods are used. (c) Documents are prepared on the model validation process and the methods of measuring risk indicators. (d) Criteria for assessing the accuracy of the expected exposure model and an improvement process are established. (e) The method of constructing the representative portfolios used in model validation is defined. (f) Where exposure models and risk indicators using forecast distributions are validated, multiple statistical distributions are used. (g) It is validated whether risk is being underestimated because the assumptions used in the expected exposure model are inappropriate. (h) In carrying out IMM backtesting, all of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) Historical data on changes in market risk are used. In this case, that data shall take into account as many forecast horizons exceeding at least one year as possible, and shall vary the initialization dates. (2) It covers the expected exposure model and the risk indicators. In this case, for collateralized transactions, the forecast horizon shall be at least one year and shall include the typical margin period of risk. (3) A method of fixing positions for representative portfolios is used. (4) It is designed to test the important assumptions of the expected exposure model and the risk indicators. (i) Valuation models are periodically validated against appropriate benchmarks. (j) It is validated that transaction-specific information is captured accurately and that transactions are allocated to the appropriate netting sets. (k) The risk factors of the expected exposure model, such as interest rates, foreign exchange, share prices and commodity prices, are forecast over a long period, and expected exposure is measured over the contractual term of all transactions included in the netting set. (l) Validation takes into account the most recent situation regarding the accuracy of the expected exposure model and the risk indicators. (m) The appropriateness of the frequency of updating the parameters used in the expected exposure model is validated. (vi) That the expected exposure management unit controls the appropriateness of the input data of the expected exposure model and analyses the information output from it (including analysis based on comparing the exposures of transactions calculated by the expected exposure model with limits). (vii) That directors, etc. are actively involved in the procedures for managing counterparty credit risk relating to expected exposure (including model validation). (viii) That the expected exposure model and the risk indicators are closely integrated into normal risk management procedures and are used in managing credit extended by the Ultimate Designated Parent Company, etc. (ix) That documents describing the internal policies, controls and procedures for operating the expected exposure model and the risk indicators (including criteria for assessing the expected exposure model and measures to be taken when those criteria are breached) have been prepared, and that means for ensuring compliance with them have been put in place. (x) That, as a rule, an internal audit is conducted at least once a year of the process of measuring counterparty credit risk relating to expected exposure and of the internal management of counterparty credit risk (including the operations of the expected exposure management unit). (xi) That transaction-specific information is obtained in order to capture the effect of margin calls. (xii) That a framework for appropriate collateral management (including that relating to the reuse of collateral) has been established, and that a unit has been set up to calculate and call collateral, manage collateral disputes, report accurately each day the individual collateral amounts and the levels of initial margin and variation margin, and regularly report information on appropriate collateral management to directors, etc. (xiii) That the expected exposure management unit has established a framework for identifying, monitoring and managing general wrong-way risk and specific wrong-way risk. (xiv) That, where cross-product netting (meaning measuring the exposure to a counterparty on a net basis by aggregating several different transactions into a single claim or obligation; the same applies hereinafter in this item) is applied to multiple repo-style transactions, or multiple margin lending and similar overseas transactions, with a single counterparty, or to derivative transactions and repo-style transactions and margin lending and similar overseas transactions with a single counterparty, all of the following requirements are satisfied: (a) The following legal requirements: (1) Where an event occurs that allows one party to terminate the transactions, the amount to be received from or paid to the counterparty is the close-out amount under the master agreement included in the legally effective netting contract plus the sum of the market values of all transactions included in that netting contract. (2) Where an event occurs that allows one party to terminate the transactions, the other party can promptly terminate all transactions subject to cross-product netting and turn them into a single claim or obligation. (3) It is confirmed on an ongoing basis that the contract relating to cross-product netting is effective in light of all laws and regulations (including foreign laws and regulations) relevant to it. (4) Where the effect of credit risk mitigation techniques is reflected, the provisions of Section 6 are followed. (5) All documents relating to the contract relating to cross-product netting are properly retained. (b) The following operational requirements: (1) The credit equivalent amount taking into account the effect of cross-product netting is integrated into normal risk management procedures. (2) The credit equivalent amount of the counterparty is reflected in managing credit extended and in calculating the amount of economic capital. (xv) That the policy on liquidity risk management takes into account the possibility of returning collateral and posting additional collateral. (xvi) That, where α is to be estimated under the provisions of Article 49, paragraph (4), the requirements listed in the items of that paragraph are satisfied. (xvii) That, where the effect of a legally effective bilateral netting contract covering derivative transactions and repo-style transactions and margin lending and similar overseas transactions is taken into account, the conditions listed in the items of Article 49, paragraph (16) are satisfied.
